correctness.rationale: On setting y=1+t/c and u=ky^δ with k=(A/B)c^δ, logarithmic differentiation gives E=(1−1/y)(p+δ/(1+u)). Its derivative has numerator H=δ²u[g(u)−y], with the stated g>1. The map t↦u has positive derivative; κ(u)=u/g(u)^δ=k(y/g)^δ along this map, so zeros of E' have the same multiplicities as those of κ−k and the opposite sign off the zeros. κ runs monotonically from zero to infinity for δ<1, and from zero to 1/p for δ=1 (neither upper endpoint is attained). For δ>1, the sign of κ' is that of C+a(1−δ)u+b(1+δ)/u, which decreases strictly from infinity to minus infinity. Thus κ has a nondegenerate maximum k_* and tends to zero at both ends. This proves the two simple zeros and the +,−,+ sign sequence below k_*, the single double derivative zero at equality with strict increase, and monotonic increase above it. The same sign argument gives a unique global maximum in each one-zero case. For p=1,δ=2, the critical u=9 gives g=13/3 and k_*=81/169; the exact factorization at k=1/3 gives y=3 and a unique positive cubic root (one sign change), whose bisection gives t≈8.419900819340 and E≈0.952304494038. The original intensity is decreasing at all t. The gap criterion quantifies existence of a suitable k; for fixed k one also needs k<k_*.
